proposed_fields.title: Prosecutors cite Trump social media posts in seeking protective order in Jan. 6 case
proposed_fields.description_short: Prosecutors cited Trump’s social media posts in seeking a discovery protective order in the 2020 election case; the filing was not a finding that the posts were crimes.
proposed_fields.description_medium: In August 2023, special counsel Jack Smith asked the court in Washington to restrict how Donald Trump and his lawyers could disclose materials received in discovery in the 2020 election case. Prosecutors cited Trump’s history of posting about people involved in his cases and pointed to a Truth Social post reading, “If you go after me, I’m coming after you.” Trump’s lawyers argued the post was political speech. The filing documents the prosecutors’ request and stated concern, not a judicial finding that the posts constituted obstruction or witness intimidation.
proposed_fields.description_long: In August 2023, prosecutors in the federal election case against Donald Trump asked a judge in Washington to impose a protective order governing the use and disclosure of discovery materials. The Justice Department argued that public disclosure of evidence such as grand-jury interviews or sealed-warrant materials could chill witnesses or affect the administration of justice. The filing cited Trump’s history of social media posts about judges, lawyers and witnesses in his cases, including a Truth Social message stating, “If you go after me, I’m coming after you.” Trump’s defense described the post as political speech and contested the request. This procedural request concerned access to evidence exchanged in discovery; it was not itself a gag order covering all public statements and did not establish that the posts were criminal conduct. Other reporting in September 2023 described a separate request to restrict statements about participants in the election case. The supplied Washington Post link is an October 2023 catalogue, but its article body was not readable in the focused review. The revised title and account describe the documented protective-order request and avoid an unsupported count of “dozens” or a legal conclusion about obstruction. A final order should be consulted before describing the precise restrictions imposed.

uncertainty: The prosecutor’s concern and request are not a judicial finding of obstruction or witness intimidation; the supplied catalogue article does not support a verified “dozens” count in this review.

proposed_fields.title: Trump Said Arizona Officials Were Trying to Steal the 2022 Election Amid Tabulator Problems
proposed_fields.description_short: Trump said Arizona officials were trying to steal the election after Maricopa County reported ballot-machine problems.
proposed_fields.description_medium: On November 8, 2022, Donald Trump posted that Maricopa County voting machines were not counting ballots and said, “They are trying to steal the election with bad Machines and DELAY.” Reuters reported printer and tabulator problems at some vote centers. A judge rejected a request to extend voting hours, finding no evidence that voters had been prevented from casting ballots. The equipment failures do not establish fraud or a stolen result.
proposed_fields.description_long: During Election Day on November 8, 2022, Maricopa County reported problems with ballot-on-demand printers and tabulators at some vote centers. Donald Trump used the reports to make a specific public accusation. In a post that afternoon he said some machines were not counting votes, then wrote: “People of Arizona: Don’t get out of line until you cast your vote. They are trying to steal the election with bad Machines and DELAY.” Reuters reported the machine problems and the fraud claims made by Trump and other election deniers. In a related court proceeding, a judge rejected a Republican request to extend polling hours because the party had not shown that voters were prevented from casting ballots. Maricopa County’s post-election report documents equipment problems and how ballots were handled; those problems are not evidence that votes were changed or that the election was stolen. The original title’s reference to midterm losses is misleading because Trump’s cited post was made before the results were known. This draft records the statement and the verified dispute without endorsing its allegation.

uncertainty: Trump’s post is an allegation, not proof of fraud; it preceded final results, so “midterm losses were stolen” misstates the timing.

proposed_fields.title: Trump Order Directs Federal Agencies to Restrict Gender-Affirming Care for Minors
proposed_fields.description_short: Executive Order 14187 directs federal agencies to restrict federal support and coverage for gender-affirming care for people under 19.
proposed_fields.description_medium: On January 28, 2025, Trump signed Executive Order 14187, which defines “child” as a person under 19 and directs agencies to restrict federal support for specified gender-affirming treatments. Human Rights Watch says the order targets federal funding for institutions providing or researching care and calls for limits through federal health programs. The sources do not support the original claim that a complete nationwide criminal ban was enacted.
proposed_fields.description_long: On January 28, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14187, titled “Protecting Children from Chemical and Surgical Mutilation.” The order defines a child as a person under 19 and describes puberty blockers, certain hormones and some surgical procedures as the care it seeks to restrict. It directs federal agencies to take steps involving grants and federal health programs, including TRICARE, and instructs the attorney general to prioritize enforcement of laws the order says prohibit or limit the procedures. Human Rights Watch’s June 2025 report describes the order as restricting federal funding for institutions that provide or research gender-affirming care and cutting off access through federal programs. These provisions support an account of the administration’s federal restrictions and policy direction. They do not establish that every form of care was eliminated nationwide, that providers were criminally prohibited from offering care, or that a complete federal ban had taken effect. The narrower title and description therefore identify the signed order and its stated directives without claiming universal implementation or consequences beyond the cited sources.

uncertainty: The order is not a complete nationwide criminal ban; agency directives do not prove all implementation steps occurred.
